title: Quasi-affine scheme morphisms descend along fpqc coverings
statement: Let $f:Y\to U$ be a morphism of schemes [def-pc-scheme], in the universes of [def-weil-size-convention], and let $\{p_i:U_i\to U\}_{i\in I}$ be an fpqc covering [def-weil-pbc-fpqc-covering]. Suppose that for every $i$ the base-change morphism $Y\times_UU_i\to U_i$ [def-pc-fibre-product] is quasi-affine [def-nagata-quasi-affine-morphism]. Then $f$ is quasi-affine. Here a morphism is quasi-affine when the inverse image of every affine open of its target is a quasi-affine scheme, meaning a quasi-compact open subscheme of an affine scheme [def-weil-open-immersion, def-weil-pbc-quasi-compact-scheme, def-weil-affine-spectrum]. No separation, Noetherian, finite-type or finite-presentation hypothesis is imposed on $f$ or on the base.

proof.text: Fix an affine open $V\subseteq U$ and put $X=Y\times_U V$. It suffices to show that $X$ is quasi-affine for each such $V$, by the definition of a quasi-affine morphism. Base change the given covering to $V$. The fpqc covering definition supplies finitely many affine opens $B_j$ in its members whose images cover $V$. Put $B=\coprod_{j=1}^m B_j$, with induced map $g:B\to V$. The coproduct node gives its disjoint open components, and finite-disjoint-union affineness makes $B$ affine. Each $B_j\to V$ is flat: its local-ring maps are those of the covering map. Thus $g$ is flat, by the pointwise definition of flatness, and surjective because the component images cover $V$. Since both schemes are affine, $g$ is affine and hence quasi-compact. The case $m=0$ forces $V=\varnothing$ and then $X=\varnothing$, which is a quasi-compact open subscheme of an affine scheme, so assume $m>0$.

source.place: Tag 02L7 (lemma-descending-property-quasi-affine), affine refinement of the covering; fpqc-family definition and Tag 01I5 (schemes-lemma-disjoint-union-affines).

proof.text: Write $W=X\times_V B$ and $W_j=X\times_V B_j$. The quasi-affine base-change lemma applied to the original $Y\times_U U_i\to U_i$ and $B_j\to U_i$ makes $W_j\to B_j$ quasi-affine; since $B_j$ is affine, $W_j$ is a quasi-affine scheme. By the canonical affine-embedding node each $W_j$ is quasi-compact and has an open immersion into $\operatorname{Spec}\Gamma(W_j,\mathcal O)$. The inverse images in $W$ of the disjoint open components $B_j$ cover $W$ and are exactly $W_j$, so the coproduct mapping property identifies $W$ with $\coprod_j W_j$. The component embeddings give an open immersion of this coproduct into $\coprod_j\operatorname{Spec}\Gamma(W_j,\mathcal O)$: the target components are disjoint opens and on each component it is the stated open immersion. The target is affine by finite-disjoint-union affineness, and $W$ is quasi-compact since an open covering restricts to coverings of the finitely many quasi-compact $W_j$. Hence $W$ is quasi-affine. It is therefore separated and quasi-compact as a scheme. Cancellation of separatedness gives that $W\to B$ is separated; qcqs morphism permanence gives that it is quasi-compact, since $B$ is affine and thus quasi-separated.

source.place: Tag 02L7, first paragraph: quasi-affine pullbacks are quasi-compact and separated; Tags 01P9 (properties-lemma-quasi-affine) and 01I5 for the finite affine refinement.

proof.text: Apply fpqc descent of quasi-compactness and separatedness to $X\to V$ and the flat surjective quasi-compact map $B\to V$. Step 2 verifies both hypotheses on $W\to B$, so $X\to V$ is quasi-compact and separated. A separated morphism is quasi-separated. The affine scheme $V$ is quasi-compact and quasi-separated, so qcqs morphism permanence now shows that the scheme $X$ is quasi-compact and quasi-separated. These are the hypotheses needed for flat base change; no quasi-compactness of $U$ or of $Y$ has been assumed.

source.place: Tag 02L7, first paragraph, using Tags 02KQ and 02KU (lemma-descending-property-quasi-compact, lemma-descending-property-separated).

proof.text: Put $R=\Gamma(V,\mathcal O)$, $R'=\Gamma(B,\mathcal O)$, $C=\Gamma(X,\mathcal O)$, and $D=\operatorname{Spec}C$. The identity of $C$ defines $j:X\to D$; the ring map $R\to C$ makes it a $V$-morphism. Flat base change gives the specific ring isomorphism $\beta:C\otimes_R R'\xrightarrow{\sim}\Gamma(W,\mathcal O)$, $c\otimes b\mapsto c|_W\,b|_W$. The affine fibre-product node identifies $D\times_V B$ with $\operatorname{Spec}(C\otimes_RR')$. The pullback $j_B:W\to D\times_V B$ corresponds under the morphism-into-affine bijection to precisely $\beta$: on the two tensor factors its section map is pullback of $c$ from $X$ and of $b$ from $B$, and multiplication gives the displayed formula. Thus, after the spectrum isomorphism induced by $\beta$, $j_B$ is the canonical map $W\to\operatorname{Spec}\Gamma(W,\mathcal O)$. Since $W$ is quasi-affine by step 2, its canonical affine embedding is an open immersion.

source.place: Tag 02L7, middle paragraph, specializing the canonical relative spectrum to affine V; Tag 02KH (coherent-lemma-flat-base-change-cohomology), i=0, and Tag 01P9.

proof.text: The projection $D\times_V B\to D$ is flat and surjective by base change of these properties of $g$, and both its source and target are affine. Apply affine open-immersion descent to $j:X\to D$ and this projection. Its pullback is $j_B$ by the fibre-product universal property, so step 4 proves the required open-immersion hypothesis. Consequently $j$ is an open immersion. Its source $X$ is quasi-compact by step 3, so its image is a quasi-compact open subscheme of the affine scheme $D$. Hence $X$ is quasi-affine. This works for every affine open $V\subseteq U$, and the defining condition says that $f$ is quasi-affine.

source.place: Tag 02L7, final paragraph: descent of the canonical open immersion by Tag 02L3 (lemma-descending-property-open-immersion), followed by the definition of quasi-affineness.

proof_origin.place: Tag 02L7 (lemma-descending-property-quasi-affine), proof, using its affine-chart form and the explicit flat base-change map of Tag 02KH.
